summary_html: Immediate state action to **protect a child in imminent danger**. Federal law (ASFA/IV-E) ties funding to court findings on **reasonable efforts**, and constitutional limits (due process, 4th/14th Amendments) constrain warrantless removals.
authority_html:
- **ASFA / SSA Title IV-E** — reasonable-efforts findings; permanency timelines  
- **CFSR (45 CFR Part 1355)** — federal oversight of removal decision quality  
- **Constitutional constraints** — enforced via §1983 actions; due process & search/seizure jurisprudence (not listed in file but governs practice)

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.holding: The South Carolina Supreme Court upheld the emergency protective custody statute against state and federal constitutional challenge, held that orders issued after a merits hearing are final and must be timely appealed, and affirmed termination of parental rights and the adoption.
key_cases.relevance: It is the leading South Carolina case on emergency protective custody and expressly rests the statute's constitutionality on its deadlines and procedural safeguards.
key_cases.quote: We further conclude that S.C.Code Ann. § 20-7-610(A) (Supp.1997) does not violate the state or federal constitutions.

key_cases.case_name: South Carolina Department of Social Services v. Randy S.
key_cases.court: Court of Appeals of South Carolina
key_cases.holding: The court held that where DSS in substance removed children and placed them with a relative, it had brought a removal action and was required to follow the removal procedures — petition, 72-hour probable cause hearing, 35-day merits hearing — rather than proceeding as an intervention.
key_cases.relevance: This is the clearest South Carolina roadmap of the EPC timeline from § 63-7-620 through the probable cause and merits hearings.
key_cases.quote: Despite DSS's contention that this was only an intervention action, we find the evidence supports a finding that Children were removed from Father's custody.

key_cases.case_name: South Carolina Department of Social Services v. Gamble
key_cases.court: Court of Appeals of South Carolina
key_cases.holding: The court reversed dismissal of a removal case, holding the statute requires that the merits hearing be scheduled to be held — not necessarily completed — within thirty-five days of the removal petition, and rejecting the parent's constitutional challenge.
key_cases.relevance: Gamble is the controlling construction of the 35-day merits hearing deadline that follows emergency protective custody.
key_cases.quote: The statute requires the family court to schedule a hearing on the merits to be held within thirty-five days of the removal petition.

key_cases.case_name: Jordan ex rel. Jordan v. Jackson
key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The Fourth Circuit upheld an emergency protective custody statute facially and as applied, holding that a 65-hour delay between emergency removal and judicial review did not violate due process while warning that it approached the outer limit.
key_cases.relevance: Jordan fixes the federal ceiling on how long a child may be held in emergency protective custody before a judge reviews the removal, which South Carolina's 72-hour probable-cause rule in S.C. Code § 63-7-710(A) sits right against.
key_cases.quote: We believe this period is near, if not at, the outer limit of permissible delay between a child's removal from his home and judicial review.

key_cases.case_name: White Ex Rel. White v. Chambliss
key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The Fourth Circuit held South Carolina DSS officials were entitled to qualified immunity on claims arising from the removal of children and the foster placement in which one child died, because no clearly established federal right — including any right created by the South Carolina Child Protection Act — was violated.
key_cases.relevance: Emergency custody decisions by SC DSS staff are judged by White's qualified-immunity standard, which tolerates good-faith discretionary judgments.
key_cases.quote: The facts presented by White reveal that the DSS defendants violated no "clearly established" law in removing White's children from her custody.

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Court held that an unwed father is entitled as a matter of due process to a hearing on his fitness before his children may be taken from him, and that denying him the hearing extended to all other parents denied him the equal protection of the laws.
key_cases.relevance: It is the constitutional origin of the rule that protective custody must be followed by an individualized judicial determination of parental fitness rather than a statutory presumption of unfitness.
key_cases.quote: We conclude that, as a matter of due process of law, Stanley was entitled to a hearing on his fitness as a parent before his children were taken from him

mandatory_reporters: Listed professionals only, acting in their professional capacity (South Carolina is not a universal-reporter state) — S.C. Code Ann. § 63-7-310(A)
Physicians, nurses, dentists, optometrists, medical examiners, coroners, and employees of a county medical examiner's or coroner's office
Any other medical, emergency medical services, mental health, or allied health professional
Members of the clergy, including Christian Science practitioners and religious healers
Clerical or nonclerical religious counselors who charge for services
School teachers, counselors, principals, assistant principals, and school attendance officers
Childcare workers in a childcare center or foster care facility
Undertakers, funeral home directors, and employees of a funeral home
Volunteer non-attorney guardians ad litem serving on behalf of the South Carolina Guardian ad Litem Program or Richland County CASA
Any other person may report and is encouraged to report — S.C. Code Ann. § 63-7-310(D)

other: Encourages, condones, or approves the commission of delinquent acts by the child and those acts are shown to be the result of the encouragement, condonation, or approval
